verses.zh: 我见日光之下有一宗祸患重压在人身上，
verses.en: Here is[NOTE:1] another misfortune[NOTE:2] that I have seen on earth,[NOTE:3] and it weighs heavily[NOTE:4] on people:[NOTE:5]
notes: The term יֵשׁ (yesh, “there is”) is often used in aphorisms to assert the existence of a particular situation that occurs sometimes. It may indicate that the situation is not the rule but that it does occur on occasion, and may be nuanced “sometimes” (Prov 11:24; 13:7, 23; 14:12; 16:25; 18:24; 20:15; Eccl 2:21; 4:8; 5:12; 6:1; 7:15 [2x]; 8:14 [3x]).
The noun רָעָה (raʿah, “evil”) probably means “misfortune” (HALOT 1263 s.v. רָעָה 4) or “injustice, wrong” (HALOT 1262 s.v. רָעָה 2.b); see, e.g., Eccl 2:17; 5:12, 15; 6:1; 10:5.
Heb “under the sun.”
The word “weighs” does not appear in Hebrew, but is added in the translation for smoothness.

Heb “it is great upon men.” The phrase וְרַבָּה הִיא עַל־הָאָדָם (verabbah hiʾ ʿal-haʾadam) is taken in two basic ways: (1) commonality: “it is common among men” (KJV, MLB), “it is prevalent among men” (NASB), “that is frequent among men” (Douay). (2) oppressiveness: “it lies heavy upon men” (RSV, NRSV), “it weighs heavily upon men” (NEB, NAB, NIV), “it presses heavily on men” (Moffatt), “it is heavy upon men” (ASV), and “a grave one it is for man” (NJPS). The preposition עַל (ʿal, “upon”) argues against the first in favor of the second; the notion of commonality would be denoted by the preposition ב (bet, “among”). The singular noun אָדָם (ʾadam) is used as a collective, denoting “men.” The article on הָאָדָם (haʾadam) is used in a generic sense referring to humankind as a whole; the generic article is often used with a collective singular (IBHS 244 §13.5.1f).
verses.commentary:
6:1

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta
"an evil"

TEV
"a serious injustice"

NJB, NIV
"another evil"

This is the Hebrew term (BDB 948 II, KB 1250 I) that has been used often by Qoheleth. It starts
Eccl. 6:1 (evil) and closes Eccl. 6:2. See note at Eccl. 2:21 and especially at Eccl. 5:13.

▣ "under the sun" This is referring to human values and perspectives only. See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

NASB
"it is prevalent"

NKJV, Peshitta
"it is common"

NRSV
"it lies heavy"

NJB
"which goes hard with people"

LXX
"it is abundant"

REB, NIV
"it weighs heavily"

JPSOA
"a grave one"

This is the ADJECTIVE (BDB 915 I, KB 1176) and a
DEMONSTRATIVE ADJECTIVE (BDB 214). As the translations show there
are two ways to interpret this phrase:

- The evil is common to all humans. (Peshitta)

- The evil weighs heavily on humans (MT).

verses.zh: 就是人蒙　神赐他资财、丰富、尊荣，以致他心里所愿的一样都不缺，只是　神使他不能吃用，反有外人来吃用。这是虚空，也是祸患。
verses.en: God gives a man riches, property, and wealthso that he lacks nothing that his heart[NOTE:1] desires,[NOTE:2] yet God does not enable[NOTE:3] him to enjoy[NOTE:4] the fruit of his labor[NOTE:5]—instead, someone else[NOTE:6] enjoys[NOTE:7] it![NOTE:8] This is fruitless and a grave misfortune.[NOTE:9]
notes: Heb “his appetite.”
Heb “There is no lack in respect to his appetite”; or “his desire lacks nothing.”

The verb שָׁלַט (shalat) in the Qal stem means “to domineer; to dominate; to lord it over; to be master of” and in the Hiphil stem “to give power to” (BDB 1020 s.v. שָׁלַט) and “to grant” (HALOT 1522 s.v. שׁלט). God must grant a person the ability to enjoy the fruit of his labor, otherwise a person will not be able to enjoy his possessions and wealth. The ability to partake of the fruit of one’s labor and to find satisfaction and joy in it is a gift from God (e.g., Eccl 2:24-26; 3:13; 5:18 [19]; 9:7).

Heb “to eat of it.” The verb אָכַל (ʾakhal, “to eat”) functions as a metonymy of association, that is, the action of eating is associated with the enjoyment of the fruit of one’s labor (e.g., Eccl 2:24-26; 3:12-13, 22; 5:17-19; 8:15; 9:9).
The phrase “the fruit of his labor” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.

Heb “a stranger.” The Hebrew expression אִיש נָכְרִי (ʾish nokhri, “stranger”) sometimes refers not to a foreigner or someone that the person does not know, but simply to someone else other than the subject (e.g., Prov 27:2). In the light of 6:3-6, it might even refer to the man’s own heirs. The term is used as a synecdoche of species (foreigner for stranger) in the sense of someone else other than the subject: “someone else” (BDB 649 s.v. נָכְרִי 3).
Heb “eats.”

Instead, someone else enjoys it. A person may be unable to enjoy the fruit of his/her labor due to an unfortunate turn of events that robs a person of his possessions (5:13-14) or a miserly, lifelong hoarding of one’s wealth that robs him of the ability to enjoy what he has worked so hard to acquire (5:15-17). Qoheleth recommends the enjoyment of life and the fruit of one’s labor, as God enables (5:18-20). Unfortunately, the ability to enjoy the fruits of one’s labor is often thwarted by the obstacles described in 6:1-2 and 6:3-9.
Heb “an evil sickness.”
verses.commentary:
6:2 "a man" This is not the term adam (BDB 9), as in Eccl. 5:19, but ish (BDB 35). These two
terms for humanity have

- slightly different root meanings

- significant semantic overlap

In Ecclesiastes they are synonymous (cf. 2 Kgs. 7:10).

▣ "God has given" This refers to the sovereignty of God in human life and daily affairs
(cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:14; 5:19). However, His activity is exactly opposite to traditional wisdom (cf. Job's three
friends). Mosaic revelation promised abundance for covenant obedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deutrtonomy 28; 30:15,19),
but Qoheleth had seen the prosperity of the wicked (cf. Psalm 73). The traditional theology of "the two ways" did
not cover all of life (cf. Job).

▣ "riches. . .wealth. . .honor" See 2 Chr. 1:11, which shows that these things are the desires
of all humans. We think these things will make us happy so we pursue them with all our strength and
mental focus, but they do not, cannot (i.e., Jer. 9:23-24)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

▣ "God has given. . .God has not empowered" Notice the active presence of God. In Eccl. 5:19
this presence is a blessing ("given" and "empowered"), but here the blessing of material possessions is
not balanced with the wisdom to enjoy them! Things, without inner peace, do not bring happiness, contentment,
satisfaction, or lasting benefit!

We need to:

- enjoy daily life, whatever it may bring (i.e., Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18-20; 7:7-9)

- trust in eternal life, whenever and however physical life ceases (i.e., Eccl. 1:3; 3:9; 5:16; 6:11)

- honor God (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12)!

- obey God (cf. Eccl. 12:13)!

▣ "soul lacks nothing of all that he desires" See Ps. 17:14; 73:7; Luke 12:19. For notes
on nephesh (i.e., soul) see Lev. 17:11 and Gen. 35:18 online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

▣ "to eat from" This is imagery meaning "to enjoy." Humans work hard but do not enjoy the fruit of their labors.

▣ "foreigner" This (BDB 648, KB 700 II) can refer to

- war/invasion

- one who is not related by birth (JPSOA)

- imagery of the frailty of wealth in this world

In Israel's history it refers to Moses' curses of covenant disobedience in Leviticus 26;
Deuteronomy 28.

NASB
"sore affliction"

NKJV
"an evil affliction"

NRSV
"a grievous evil"

TEV
"just isn't right"

NJB
"grievous suffering"

LXX
"an evil infirmity"

REB
"a dire affliction"

JPSOA
"a grievous ill"

Peshitta
"an evil disease"

This is made up of a NOUN and an ADJECTIVE.

- NOUN, BDB 318, KB 318, meaning sickness, cf. Eccl. 5:16; Deut. 28:59,61; Isa. 53:4

- ADJECTIVE, BDB 948 I, KB 1250-1253, meaning injury or wrong. See note at Eccl. 5:13.

Life is unfair and unpredictable, yet God is actively present. In the Semitic proverb
genre called "role reversal" the same occurs. The seeming prosperity of the wicked (so common in our world)
will change (cf. Psalm 73). Lasting happiness and contentment sought after so diligently by godless
humans will not bring lasting satisfaction. A righteous God will act, will judge, will right the wrongs of this life (cf. Job).

▣ "vanity" See note at Eccl. 1:2.

verses.zh: 人若生一百个儿子，活许多岁数，以致他的年日甚多，心里却不得满享福乐，又不得埋葬；据我说，那不到期而落的胎比他倒好。
verses.en: Even if a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, even if he lives a long, long time,[NOTE:1] but cannot enjoy his prosperity—even if he were to live forever[NOTE:2]—I would say, “A stillborn child[NOTE:3] is better off than he is.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the days of his years are many.”

Heb “he has no burial.” The phrase וְגַם־קְבוּרָה לֹא־הָיְתָה (vegam qevurah loʾ hayetah, “he even has no burial”) is traditionally treated as part of a description of the man’s sorry final state, that is, he is deprived of even a proper burial (KJV, NEB, RSV, NRSV, ASV, NASB, NIV, NJPS, MLB, Moffatt). However, the preceding parallel lines suggest that this a hyperbolic protasis: “If he were to live one hundred years…even if he were never buried [i.e., were to live forever]….” A similar idea occurs elsewhere (e.g., Pss 49:9; 89:48). See D. R. Glenn, “Ecclesiastes,” BKCOT, 990.

The noun נֶפֶל (nefel) denotes “miscarriage” and by metonymy of effect, “stillborn child” (e.g., Ps 58:9; Job 3:16; Eccl 6:3); cf. HALOT 711. The noun is related to the verb נָפַל (nafal, “to fall,” but occasionally “to be born”; see Isa 26:18); cf. HALOT 710 s.v. נפל 5.
The point of 6:3-6 is that the futility of unenjoyed wealth is worse than the tragedy of being stillborn.
verses.commentary:
6:3-6 The paragraph gives several specific examples which seem to go against traditional wisdom
teachings. A man may have

- many children (i.e., sexual pleasure and descendants)

- a long lifetime (i.e., health and many experiences)

- he will find no satisfaction (i.e., no lasting advantage, cf. Eccl. 1:3)

- his life has been vain, empty, meaningless (cf. Eccl. 1:2)

Almost as an aside, Qoheleth mentions, "no proper burial," which was very important to Jewish
people. The word "proper" is not in the Hebrew text. Even if he had had a proper burial without lasting
benefit, he would not be satisfied! Preparation for the afterlife is not made at death, but through life!

The NET Bible has an interesting take on this line (p. 1129). It sees it as related to the
previous line and referring to an extended life. It mentions Ps. 49:9 and 89:48 as other examples of this
poetic parallelism. I think this interpretation is surely possible and fits the immediate context well!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN AGING

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

6:3 "hundred children" This is hyperbolic and refers to the harems of royalty or the wealthy. Children are a
great blessing from God (cf. Ps. 127:3-5), but they cannot provide a lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:18).

▣ "lives many years" Long life is also a great blessing from God (cf. Prov. 3:16), but
it cannot provide a lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 6:6).

▣ "he does not have proper burial" In Hebrew this can refer to an elaborate funeral. Not to be buried properly
was a sign of shame (cf. 1 Kgs. 14:13; 2 Kgs. 9:10,35; Ps. 79:3; Eccl. 6:3; Isa. 14:19-20; Jer. 8:2; 14:16; 16:4; 23:33).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CRUCIFIXION, IV.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

▣ "Better the miscarriage than he" This is based on the life of a man mentioned in Eccl. 6:1-3.
This world's goods and honors (cf. chapters 1-2) do not, by themselves, bring happiness or lasting benefit
(cf. Eccl. 4:3). Life without God is not authentic life!

The term "miscarriage" (BDB 658, KB 711) can mean

- abortive birth, cf. Job 3:16; Ps. 58:8; NRSV

- untimely (i.e., early or late) birth (RSV)

Number 1 fits this context best (cf. Eccl. 4:3).

For "better" see notes at Eccl. 5:18 and 7:1.

verses.zh: 因为虚虚而来，暗暗而去，名字被黑暗遮蔽，
verses.en: Though the stillborn child[NOTE:1] came into the world[NOTE:2] for no reason[NOTE:3] and departed into darkness,though its name is shrouded in darkness,[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (“the stillborn child”) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The phrase “into the world” does not appear in Hebrew, but is added in the translation for clarity.
The birth of the stillborn was in vain—it did it no good to be born.
The name of the stillborn is forgotten.
verses.commentary:
6:4-5 "it" This refers to the untimely birth of Eccl. 6:3.

- Its birth is in vain.

- It goes into obscurity (darkness).

- Its name is covered in obscurity (darkness).

- It never sees the sun (i.e., light).

- It never has wisdom.

- It is better off!

What a pessimistic view of human life! This challenges OT Wisdom teaching! This author wants us to walk to the
brink of existence and look straight into the empty nothingness of atheistic humanism!

For "darkness" see note at Eccl. 5:17.

verses.zh: 并且没有见过天日，也毫无知觉；这胎，比那人倒享安息。
verses.en: though it never saw the light of day[NOTE:1] nor knew anything,[NOTE:2] yet it has more rest[NOTE:3] than that man—
notes: Heb “saw the sun.”
The word “anything” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew term translated rest here refers to freedom from toil, anxiety, and misery—part of the miserable misfortune that the miserly man of wealth must endure.
verses.commentary:
6:5 "never sees the sun" This is an idiom for human life (cf. Ps. 58:8; Eccl. 6:5; 7:11), someone who experiences
life on this planet.

▣

NASB, JPSOA
"it is better off than he"

NKJV
"this has more rest than that man"

NRSV
"yet it finds rest rather than he"

TEV
"but at least it has found rest"

NJB
"it will rest more easily than that person"

LXX, Peshitta
"yet this one has more rest than the other"

The "it" refers to the child of untimely birth, which is contrasted with the man
who has wealth and honor, but no peace, Eccl. 6:1-3.

verses.zh: 那人虽然活千年，再活千年，却不享福，众人岂不都归一个地方去吗？
verses.en: if he should live a thousand years twice, yet does not enjoy his prosperity.For both of them die![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “Do not all go to the same place?” The rhetorical question is an example of erotesis of positive affirmation, expecting a positive answer, e.g., Ps 56:13 [14] (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 947). It affirms the fact that both the miserly rich man who lives two thousand years, as well as the stillborn who never lived one day, both go to the same place—the grave. And if the miserly rich man never enjoyed the fruit of his labor during his life, his fate was no better than that of the stillborn who never had opportunity to enjoy any of the blessings of life. In a sense, it would have been better for the miserly rich man to have never lived than to have experienced the toil, anxiety, and misery of accumulating his wealth, but never enjoying any of the fruits of his labor.
verses.commentary:
6:6 "thousand years" This is a symbol of fullness or completeness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣ "do not all go to one place" This refers to the common fate of all living things, Sheol
(cf. Eccl. 2:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD? I. B.

verses.zh: 人的劳碌都为口腹，心里却不知足。
verses.en: All man’s labor is for nothing more than[NOTE:1] to fill his stomach[NOTE:2]—yet his appetite[NOTE:3] is never satisfied!
notes: The phrase “for nothing more than” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.

Heb “All man’s work is for his mouth.” The term “mouth” functions as a synecdoche of part (i.e., mouth) for the whole (i.e., person), substituting the organ of consumption for the person’s action of consumption (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 641-43), as suggested by the parallelism with נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “his appetite”).
The term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “desire; appetite”) is used as a metonymy of association, that is, the soul is associated with man’s desires and appetites (BDB 660 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 5.c; 6.a).
verses.commentary:
6:7-9 This may be poetry (cf. NJB). The parallel lines would be:

- all animals toil just to eat (cf. Gen. 3:17-19); yet they can never eat enough to give lasting
satisfaction (i.e., they get hungry again), Eccl. 6:7

- both the wise and the foolish are caught up in the trials and problems of a fallen world. The second line
is uncertain; it seems to give an advantage (i.e., "street smarts") to the poor man who has to
perpetually cope with less, Eccl. 6:8

- all humans want more than they have, yet when they have much (i.e., chapters 1-2) it is still
not enough (i.e., vanity, futility, see note at Eccl. 1:14), Eccl. 6:9

verses.zh: 这样看来，智慧人比愚昧人有甚么长处呢？穷人在众人面前知道如何行，有甚么长处呢？
verses.en: So what advantage does a wise man have over a fool?[NOTE:1] And what advantage[NOTE:2] does a pauper gain by knowing how to survive?[NOTE:3]
notes: So what advantage does the wise man have over a fool? The rhetorical question in Hebrew implies a negative answer: the wise man has no absolute advantage over a fool in the sense that both will share the same fate: death. Qoheleth should not be misunderstood here as denying that wisdom has no relative advantage over folly; elsewhere he affirms that wisdom does yield some relative benefits in life (7:1-22). However, wisdom cannot deliver one from death.
As in the preceding parallel line, this rhetorical question implies a negative answer (see the note after the word “fool” in the preceding line).
Heb “ What to the pauper who knows to walk before the living”; or “how to get along in life.”
verses.commentary:
6:8 "advantage" This term (BDB 452, KB 404 cf. Eccl. 6:8,11) is a recurrent key word in Ecclesiastes.
See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

▣ "the wise man have over the fool?" There is a helpful comment in NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 1282.

"He queries whether there is any quantitative 'better' that distinguishes sage from fool, righteous from wicked,
human from beast. Both wise and foolish must die, and neither is remembered for long. Ultimately, even wisdom is futile (2:12-17; 6:8)."

verses.zh: 眼睛所看的比心里妄想的倒好。这也是虚空，也是捕风。
verses.en: It is better to be content with[NOTE:1] what the eyes can see[NOTE:2] than for one’s heart always to crave more.[NOTE:3] This continual longing[NOTE:4] is futile—like[NOTE:5] chasing the wind.
notes: The phrase “to be content with” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.

The expression מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם (marʾeh ʿenayim, “the seeing of the eyes”) is a metonymy of cause (i.e., seeing an object) for effect (i.e., being content with what the eyes can see); see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 552-54.

Heb “the roaming of the soul.” The expression מֵהֲלָךְ־נָפֶשׁ (mehalakh nafesh, “the roaming of the soul”) is a metonymy for unfulfilled desires. The term “soul” (נֶפֶשׁ, nefesh) is used as a metonymy of association for man’s desires and appetites (BDB 660 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 5.c; 6.a). This also involves the personification of the roving appetite as “roving” (מֵהֲלָךְ); see BDB 235 s.v. הָלַךְ II.3.f; 232 I.3.
The phrase “continual longing” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.
The term “like” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity and smoothness.

verses.zh: 先前所有的，早已起了名，并知道何为人，他也不能与那比自己力大的相争。
verses.en: Whatever has happened was foreordained,[NOTE:1] and what happens to a person[NOTE:2] was also foreknown.It is useless for him to argue with God about his fatebecause God is more powerful than he is.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “already its name was called.”
Or “and what a person (Heb “man”) is was foreknown.”

Heb “he cannot contend with the one who is more powerful than him.” The referent of the “the one who is more powerful than he is” (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity. The words “with God about his fate” have been added for clarity as well.
verses.commentary:
6:10 "named" This is either:

- a reference to the naming of the animals by Adam, showing his dominion or authority over them
(cf. Gen. 2:19-20)

- a reference to man being named "Adam" from the Hebrew Adamah (cf. Gen. 2:18-25)

- However, in this context it is not the naming of Adam or Adam naming the animals that is the focus, but the repetitive
cycle (cf. Eccl. 1:9; 3:15) of humans naming things. This naming was, in a sense, an act of power and authority. Adam
had dominion (cf. Gen. 1:28-30), but lost it (i.e., Genesis 3).

▣ "for he cannot dispute with him who is stronger than he is" The "him who is stronger" can refer to:

- another human (i.e., one person seeks justice from a physically or socially stronger person, cf. NJB)

- imagery of the cycles of time, which have already named everything (over and over)

- God (cf. Job 9:32; 40:2; Isa. 45:9)

Number 3 fits the context best.

verses.zh: 加增虚浮的事既多，这与人有甚么益处呢？
verses.en: The more one argues with words, the less he accomplishes.[NOTE:1] How does that benefit him?[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “The more the words, the more the futility.”
Or “What benefit does man have [in that]?”
verses.commentary:
6:11-12 Human disputation, either with God or one another, cannot solve the problem of meaningless
life without hope.

The famous question of Ecclesiastes is, "What then is the advantage to a man?" This is a
repeat of Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,22; 3:9; 5:16! Without a God of justice and mercy there is no joy, benefit,
or lasting satisfaction! Life can be good or hard, but what is beyond? Is there a qualitative difference
between the fate of a person of faith versus a self-seeking, wicked person?

Human life is fleeting (i.e., like a shadow, cf. Eccl. 8:13; 1 Chr. 29:15; Job 9:9; 14:2;
Ps. 102:11; 109:23; 144:4). Human life is a laborious toil. What does the future hold? This is the
question (cf. Eccl. 3:22; 7:14; 8:7; 10:14). Is there a fair, just, merciful, unchanging God whose
promises can be depended on? This is the faith issue of human existence!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

6:11 "many words which increase futility" The INFINITIVE "many"
(BDB 915 I, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) and
the PARTICIPLE "increase" (BDB 915 I, KB 1176,
Hiphil PARTICIPLE) are word plays on the same Hebrew root,
which means, "make much" or "make great."

Israel's Wisdom tradition counseled speaking few words (cf. Prov. 10:19 and Eccl. 5:2-3), because words
quickly reveal the person's character and motives.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

▣ "advantage" This is a major theological issue in Ecclesiastes. See full nte at Eccl. 1:3.

verses.zh: 人一生虚度的日子，就如影儿经过，谁知道甚么与他有益呢？谁能告诉他身后在日光之下有甚么事呢？
verses.en: For no one knows what is best for a person during his life[NOTE:1]—during the few days of his fleeting life—for[NOTE:2] they pass away[NOTE:3] like a shadow.Nor can anyone tell him what the future will hold for him on earth.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “For who knows what is good for a man in life?” The rhetorical question (“For who knows…?”) is a negative affirmation, expecting a negative answer: “For no one knows…!” (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 949-51). The translation renders this rhetorical device as a positive affirmation.

The vav prefixed to וְיַעֲשֵׂם (veyaʿasem, conjunction plus Qal imperfect third person masculine singular from עָשַׂה, ʿasah, “to do” plus third person masculine plural suffix) functions in an explanatory or epexegetical sense (“For…”).

The third person masculine plural suffix on the verb וְיַעֲשֵׂם (veyaʿasem, conjunction plus Qal imperfect third person masculine singular from עָשָׂה, ʿasah, “to do” plus third person masculine plural suffix) refers to מִסְפַּר יְמֵי־חַיֵּי הֶבְלוֹ (mispar yeme khayye hevlo, “the few days of his fleeting life”). The suffix may be taken as an objective genitive: “he spends them [i.e., the days of his life] like a shadow” (HALOT 891 s.v. I עָשָׂה) or as a subjective genitive: “they [i.e., the days of his life] pass like a shadow” (BDB 795 s.v. עָשָׂה II.11).

Heb “Who can tell the man what shall be after him under the sun?” The rhetorical question (“For who can tell him…?”) is a negative affirmation, expecting a negative answer: “For no one can tell him…!” (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 949-51). The translation renders this rhetorical device as a positive affirmation.

6:12 "who" Notice there are two questions introduced with "who."

▣ "like a shadow" In this context "shadow" (BDB 853) is used as imagery for the fleeting transitoriness of human
life (cf. 1 Chr. 29:15; Job 8:9; 14:1-2; Ps. 102:11; 109:23; 144:4; Eccl. 6:12; 8:13).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation
of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject
divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the
original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Ecclesiastes 6:1 through 8:15 may be a loosely structured literary unit.

- Chapter 6 begins with the folly of (hyperboles):

- riches, Eccl. 6:2

- many children, Eccl. 6:3

- long life, Eccl. 6:6

- The reason for the folly is:

- the never-ending cycle of human existence

- the fact that fallen humanity is never satisfied with physical things (cf. chapters 1-2)

- The important question about the meaning of life is asked again in Eccl. 6:12 (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 3:9;
5:16). What does it all mean? Where is the lasting profit/advantage (see note at Eccl. 1:3)?
